title: Portfolio, Career & Professional Practice
tagline: The work, presented; the career, directed.
blurb: IL-10 is the career academy: the forward-deployed career arc (discover → model → prove → integrate → operate → generalize), interview systems (technical, system design, behavioral, offers), self-knowledge through typology assessment, entrepreneurship (the Babson-informed track: curriculum map, venture building, unit economics, fundraising literacy), and the quantitative finance ladder (undergraduate prep, MIT MicroMasters in Finance, PhD-level quant and consulting prep). The portfolio is the proof; the career is the practice.

modules.title: The Forward-Deployed Career
modules.summary: The FDE career path in six moves — Discover (finding the real problem), Model and Prove (the technical core), Integrate and Operate (shipping inside the customer), Generalize (from engagement to product) — with AI-matched applications as the outcome layer, application tracking against skills earned, and interview systems (technical, system design, behavioral, offer evaluation).
objectives: Discover: find the customer's real problem beneath the stated one.
Model and prove: build the technical case with evidence.
Integrate and operate: ship inside customer constraints; transfer operations.
Generalize: turn engagement learnings into product.
Run interviews: technical, design, behavioral, offers.

notes.title: The FDE arc: discover to generalize
notes.body:
**Discover**: finding the problem — the stated problem is rarely the real one; diagnose like a doctor (symptoms → tests → diagnosis). **Model and Prove**: the technical core — prototype the risky parts first, prove with data.

**Integrate and Operate**: shipping inside the customer — their compliance, their change windows, their team operating it after you. **Generalize**: from engagement to product — which learnings compound into something reusable?

- Discovery questions: 'what happens if we do nothing?' — the problem's value lives in the answer
- Prove with the smallest decisive experiment — the FDE doesn't have quarters, they have weeks
- Generalize deliberately: not every engagement becomes product; the pattern across three does

notes.title: The outcome layer: matched applications
notes.body:
**AI-matched applications**: match your proven skills to role requirements — apply where the evidence fits, not where the title flatters. **Application tracking against skills earned**: every application cites portfolio proof.

**The feedback loop**: outcomes refine the plan — response rates by channel, interview conversion, offer terms. The funnel is the strategy document.

- Track: applied → response → screen → onsite → offer — conversion at each stage diagnoses the bottleneck
- Low response: fix the resume/portfolio. Low conversion: fix the interview system. Low offers: fix the close
- Skills-earned tracking: the catalog's nodes become resume bullets with proof links

notes.title: Interview systems
notes.body:
**Technical interviews**: DSA + domain depth — the IL-03/IL-08 preparation, timed. **System design**: the framework (requirements → estimates → API → data → scale → trade-offs) — practiced aloud.

**Behavioral: the FDE story** — STAR with forward-deployed flavor: the customer constraint, your diagnosis, the shipped outcome, the transfer. **Offer evaluation**: total comp, growth, team, the walk-away number — decided BEFORE the offer arrives.

- System design is a conversation, not a monologue — ask clarifying questions first
- Behavioral stories need numbers: 'cut deploy time 40%' beats 'improved deploys'
- The walk-away number prevents the worst negotiation mistake: accepting from desperation

cards.back: Discover → Model → Prove → Integrate → Operate → Generalize.
'What happens if we do nothing?' — the problem's value lives there.
Smallest decisive experiment — weeks, not quarters.
Low response → resume/portfolio. Low conversion → interviews. Low offers → the close.
Requirements → estimates → API → data model → scale → trade-offs. Aloud.
Decided before the offer — prevents desperation acceptance.

choices: discover: what decision will it drive? what happens without it?
quiz.explain: Discover the real problem — the dashboard is a stated solution, not necessarily the need.

quiz.q: Two weeks to prove value. Approach?
choices: smallest decisive experiment on the riskiest assumption
quiz.explain: Prove the risky part fast — evidence beats plans in short engagements.

choices: learnings that compound into reusable product across engagements
quiz.explain: Generalize = pattern across engagements becomes product.
Requirements first — designing without constraints is guessing.

choices: STAR + numbers: constraint, action, measured outcome
quiz.explain: Structure plus quantified outcomes — the FDE story format.

quiz.explain: The walk-away number is a pre-commitment — honor it.

modules.title: Self-Knowledge: The Humanmetrics Assessment
modules.summary: The Jung-typology career assessment as the self-knowledge layer: the instrument (what it measures — preferences across four dichotomies — and what it doesn't), the 16 types as working styles (not boxes), career-fit mapping (type to role-family, working-style implications, team composition), and the development plan (growing the non-preferred functions).
objectives: Take the typology instrument and interpret it as working-style data.
Map type to role-family fit — as hypothesis, not destiny.
Design team composition with complementary styles.
Write a development plan for the non-preferred functions.

notes.title: The instrument: what it measures
notes.body:
The **Jung typology** instrument measures preferences across four dichotomies: Extraversion/Introversion (energy source), Sensing/Intuition (information), Thinking/Feeling (decisions), Judging/Perceiving (lifestyle). **What it measures**: stable preferences in how you process and decide. **What it doesn't**: ability, intelligence, character, or destiny.

- Preferences ≠ abilities — an introvert can present brilliantly; it just costs more energy
- The 16 types are **working styles**, not boxes — use for insight, not identity
- Retake variance is normal — treat borderline dichotomies as flexible, not fixed

notes.title: Career-fit mapping
notes.body:
**Type to role-family mapping**: hypotheses — e.g., INTJ/INTP patterns in architecture/research, ESFJ/ENFJ in customer-facing leadership. **Working-style implications**: how you recharge, decide, and organize — design your workday around the answers.

**Team composition**: complementary styles — the visionary needs the finisher; the analyst needs the diplomat.

- Fit is about energy economics: where does the work energize vs drain you?
- No type is 'best' for tech — the industry needs all 16; the mapping is about fit, not rank
- Use it in interviews: 'I do my best deep work in...' is self-knowledge as a selling point

notes.title: The development plan
notes.body:
Growing the **non-preferred functions**: the thinker practices naming stakeholder impact; the judger practices holding ambiguity; the introvert practices visible communication.

- Development ≠ becoming another type — it's range, not replacement
- One stretch behavior per quarter — small, observable, reviewable
- The plan lives with the career plan — self-knowledge directs the FDE arc

cards.back: E/I (energy), S/N (information), T/F (decisions), J/P (lifestyle).
Measures: processing/decision preferences. Doesn't: ability, intelligence, destiny.
Working styles, not boxes — insight, not identity.
Energy economics — where work energizes vs drains. Hypothesis, not destiny.
Complementary styles — visionary + finisher, analyst + diplomat.
Range, not replacement — one stretch behavior per quarter.

quiz.q: INTP considering sales engineering. Typology says?
choices: data point: weigh the energy economics, decide informed
quiz.explain: Hypothesis, not destiny — fit is about sustainable energy, and people stretch successfully.
Borderlines are the honest answer — flexibility, not a fixed label.

quiz.q: Team of four INTJs stalls on shipping. Diagnose?
choices: missing complementary styles — add a finisher/driver
quiz.explain: Composition: analysis without execution needs its complement.

choices: frame working style: 'I do best deep work when...'
quiz.explain: Self-knowledge as a selling point — concrete, not labeled.

choices: name stakeholder impact explicitly in proposals
quiz.explain: Range: keep the analysis, add the human impact — explicitly.

modules.title: Entrepreneurship: The Babson-Informed Track
modules.summary: Venture creation informed by Babson's curriculum structure: the curriculum map (majors/minors structure, entrepreneurship as a discipline, finance/marketing/operations foundations, the curriculum audit), venture building (problem discovery, the MVP discipline, unit economics, fundraising literacy), and the contemporary practitioner-led model (what to borrow, what to avoid).
objectives: Audit the Babson curriculum map against your venture's needs.
Discover problems worth solving: pains with budgets.
Practice the MVP discipline: smallest test of the riskiest assumption.
Model unit economics; speak fundraising literacy.

notes.title: The Babson curriculum map
notes.body:
**Majors and minors structure** — the breadth+depth model. **Entrepreneurship as a discipline**: opportunity recognition, resource marshaling, risk management — teachable, not mystical.

**Finance, marketing, operations foundations**: the three literacies every founder needs — read a P&L, acquire a customer, deliver the thing.

**The curriculum audit**: map your venture's needs against the disciplines — hire or learn to cover the gaps.

- Entrepreneurship is a practice with a literature — study it like one
- The audit prevents the classic failure: brilliant product, no distribution
- Foundations first: unit economics before virality, always

notes.title: Venture building
notes.body:
**Problem discovery**: pains with budgets — the problem must hurt AND have a payer. **The MVP discipline**: the smallest test of the riskiest assumption (not the smallest product).

**Unit economics**: CAC, LTV, payback, contribution margin — LTV:CAC ≥ 3, payback < 12 months, or the model doesn't work.

**Fundraising literacy**: SAFEs/convertibles, dilution, the pitch as a story with numbers — raise from strength or don't raise.

- MVP = experiment, not product — concierge and Wizard-of-Oz count
- Unit economics before scale — scaling a broken unit is just faster dying
- Fundraising is a tactic, not a goal — default alive beats default dead

notes.title: The contemporary practitioner model
notes.body:
**Practitioner-led education**: operators teaching operators — war stories over textbooks. **The AI/founder curriculum**: building with AI leverage. **Hiring-partner integration**: the employment bridge.

**What to borrow**: practitioner instructors, project-based proof, hiring integration. **What to avoid**: credential worship, debt for signaling, curriculum as content marketing.

- Borrow the proof-of-work model — portfolios over certificates
- Avoid paying for prestige — pay for skills and network, measurably
- The founder's curriculum is the venture itself — school is the accelerator, not the destination

cards.back: Pain + budget — hurts AND has a payer.
Smallest test of the riskiest assumption — experiment, not product.
LTV:CAC ≥ 3, payback < 12 months, positive contribution margin.
Simple Agreement for Future Equity — invest now, price later. Know the cap/discount.
Can you reach profitability on current cash? Alive = yes. Plan to alive.
Borrow: proof-of-work, operators teaching. Avoid: credential worship, debt for signaling.

quiz.q: Two ideas: fun with no payer vs boring with budget. Pick?
choices: boring with budget — pains with budgets
quiz.explain: Ventures need payers — fun without budget is a hobby.

choices: concierge test: deliver manually to 10 users
quiz.explain: Test demand with the smallest decisive experiment — manual counts.

choices: broken — LTV:CAC 2 < 3; fix economics before scale
quiz.explain: Below the bar — scaling multiplies the loss.

quiz.q: Default dead with 18 months runway. Move?
choices: path to default alive: cut, grow, or raise from strength
quiz.explain: 18 months to alive-or-funded — plan it explicitly.

quiz.q: Founder can't read a P&L. Fix?
choices: learn the three literacies: finance, marketing, ops
quiz.explain: Founders need the foundations — hire to scale, not to think.

modules.title: Quantitative Finance: The Ladder
modules.summary: Undergraduate quant preparation (the mathematics prerequisite audit, probability/statistics at depth, programming for quant, the internship map), through the MIT MicroMasters in Finance (graduate-level finance courses, the proctored comprehensive exam, the degree-pathway value, preparation mapping), toward PhD-level quant and consulting preparation (research mathematics, stochastic calculus, case interviews, the career fork: desk quant vs researcher vs consultant).
objectives: Audit prerequisites: the math, probability, and programming the ladder demands.
Map internships: the on-ramps and their timelines.
Prepare the MicroMasters: graduate finance + the proctored comprehensive.
Choose the fork: desk quant, researcher, or consultant — eyes open.

notes.title: Undergraduate preparation
notes.body:
**Mathematics prerequisite audit**: calculus, linear algebra, probability — at proof level, not cookbook. **Probability and statistics at depth**: the IL-02 quant module's content, internalized.

**Programming for quant**: Python (pandas/numpy), C++ for the latency-sensitive — the two languages of the industry.

**The internship map**: sophomore → junior summer timelines; the interviews start a year before the internship.

- The audit is honest: gaps here compound — fix them before the ladder
- Probability interviews: the classic 'coins and dice' — at depth, under time
- Code interviews: implement the math — stochastic simulation in an hour

notes.title: MIT MicroMasters in Finance
notes.body:
**Graduate-level finance courses**: the real curriculum — asset pricing, derivatives, financial engineering. **The proctored comprehensive exam**: the credential's teeth — identity-verified, rigorous.

**The degree-pathway value**: credit toward the master's — the MicroMasters as an on-ramp, not just a certificate.

**Preparation mapping**: which IL-02/IL-10 nodes prepare each course — the study plan.

- The comprehensive exam is the filter — prepare like it matters, because it does
- Graduate finance is applied stochastic calculus — the math module wasn't optional
- Pathway value: do the math on credit transfer before enrolling

notes.title: PhD-level prep and the fork
notes.body:
**Research-level mathematics**: measure theory, stochastic calculus (Itô — the quant's calculus), PDEs.

**Consulting case interviews**: a parallel track — structured problem-solving, mental math, the case framework.

**The career fork**: **desk quant** (implement models, close to P&L), **researcher** (new models, publication-adjacent), **consultant** (breadth, clients, travel) — choose with eyes open.

- Itô's lemma: the chain rule for stochastic processes — the technical heart
- Desk vs research: implementation speed vs novel mathematics — different games
- Consulting: the case interview is its own sport — practice cases, not just math

cards.back: Proof-level calculus/linear algebra/probability + Python/C++ — gaps compound.
The proctored comprehensive exam — identity-verified, rigorous.
The chain rule for stochastic processes — dW² = dt. The quant's calculus.
Desk: implement models near P&L. Researcher: novel mathematics. Different games.
Structured problem-solving + mental math + framework — practice cases.
Interviews a year before — sophomore spring for junior summer.

quiz.q: Biggest predictor of quant interview success?
choices: probability at depth + mental math under time
quiz.explain: The interviews are technical — depth and speed decide.
Itô's lemma: d(W²) = 2W dW + dt — the dt term is the whole point.

choices: degree-pathway credit — do the transfer math
quiz.explain: Credit toward the master's — verify transfer before enrolling.
Desk quants ship models that trade — speed and correctness under pressure.
Structure before solving — the framework is the answer's skeleton.

scriptLabs.title: The Application Funnel Tracker
scriptLabs.brief: Build the funnel tracker: applications in, conversion at each stage, bottleneck diagnosis. The feedback loop as code.
scriptLabs.starter:
stages = ['applied','response','screen','onsite','offer']
counts = {'applied': 40, 'response': 12, 'screen': 8, 'onsite': 3, 'offer': 1}
# TODO: print conversion rate between consecutive stages
# TODO: print overall applied->offer rate
# TODO: diagnose the bottleneck (lowest conversion stage)
scriptLabs.solution:
stages = ['applied','response','screen','onsite','offer']
counts = {'applied': 40, 'response': 12, 'screen': 8, 'onsite': 3, 'offer': 1}
convs = {}
for i in range(len(stages)-1):
    r = counts[stages[i+1]]/counts[stages[i]]
    convs[f'{stages[i]}->{stages[i+1]}'] = r
    print(f'{stages[i]} -> {stages[i+1]}: {r:.1%}')
print(f'overall: {counts["offer"]/counts["applied"]:.1%}')
bottleneck = min(convs, key=convs.get)
print(f'bottleneck: {bottleneck} ({convs[bottleneck]:.1%})')
print('low response->resume/portfolio; low conversion->interviews; low offers->the close')
# Lesson: the funnel diagnoses itself — fix the bottleneck stage, not everything.

scriptLabs.title: Unit Economics Calculator
scriptLabs.brief: Model a venture's unit economics: CAC, LTV, payback, contribution margin. Verdict: scale, fix, or kill.
scriptLabs.starter:
cac = 120          # customer acquisition cost
arpu_mo = 25       # monthly revenue per user
margin = 0.8       # gross margin
churn_mo = 0.05    # monthly churn
# TODO: LTV, LTV:CAC, payback months, verdict
scriptLabs.hint: LTV = arpu*margin/churn. payback = cac/(arpu*margin). Bar: ratio>=3, payback<12.
scriptLabs.solution:
cac = 120
arpu_mo = 25
margin = 0.8
churn_mo = 0.05
ltv = arpu_mo*margin/churn_mo
ratio = ltv/cac
payback = cac/(arpu_mo*margin)
print(f'LTV=${ltv:.0f}  LTV:CAC={ratio:.1f}  payback={payback:.1f} mo')
if ratio >= 3 and payback < 12:
    print('verdict: SCALE — economics work')
elif ratio >= 2:
    print('verdict: FIX — improve retention or monetization before scale')
else:
    print('verdict: KILL or rebuild — scaling multiplies the loss')
# Lesson: unit economics before scale — the spreadsheet is the strategy.

scriptLabs.title: The Offer Evaluator
scriptLabs.brief: Score competing offers on total comp, growth, team, and your walk-away number. Decide like an adult, not from desperation.
scriptLabs.starter:
offers = [
    {'name':'A','base':95000,'bonus':10000,'equity_yr':15000,'growth':7,'team':8},
    {'name':'B','base':110000,'bonus':5000,'equity_yr':0,'growth':5,'team':6},
]
walk_away_total = 110000
# TODO: total comp per offer; score = total/walk_away weighted with growth, team
# TODO: print ranked recommendation
scriptLabs.solution:
offers = [
    {'name':'A','base':95000,'bonus':10000,'equity_yr':15000,'growth':7,'team':8},
    {'name':'B','base':110000,'bonus':5000,'equity_yr':0,'growth':5,'team':6},
]
walk_away_total = 110000
ranked = []
for o in offers:
    total = o['base']+o['bonus']+o['equity_yr']
    score = 0.6*(total/walk_away_total) + 0.2*(o['growth']/10) + 0.2*(o['team']/10)
    ranked.append((score, o['name'], total))
    print(f"{o['name']}: total=${total:,} score={score:.2f} {'BELOW WALK-AWAY' if total < walk_away_total else ''}")
for score, name, total in sorted(ranked, reverse=True):
    print(f'rank: {name} ({score:.2f})')
# Lesson: the walk-away number, decided in advance, prevents the worst mistake.

scenarios.title: The Discovery Call
scenarios.context: Prospect: 'We need an AI chatbot for support.' Budget approved. Timeline aggressive.

options.why: Building the stated solution skips discovery — the expensive mistake.

options.text: Discover: ticket volumes, resolution rates, what 'support' costs today, what happens if nothing changes
options.why: Diagnose before prescribing — the real problem might be documentation, triage, or staffing, not a chatbot.

steps.prompt: Discovery finds 70% of tickets are password resets. Now?

options.why: The budget was for a solution; the problem is password resets — self-service reset beats a chatbot.

options.text: Reframe: propose the smallest decisive fix (self-service reset) and prove it on a pilot
options.why: FDE value: solve the real problem, prove it fast — trust compounds from honesty.

scenarios.title: Two Offers
scenarios.context: Offer A: $95k + growth. Offer B: $115k, on-call heavy, stagnant stack. Walk-away: $100k total.

options.why: Total comp isn't total value — on-call and stagnation have prices too.

options.text: Score both against walk-away + growth + team; negotiate B's terms or take A deliberately
options.why: The rubric decides, not the salary line — growth and sustainability compound.

steps.prompt: B won't budge on on-call. A counters to $102k. Move?

options.text: Take A — clears walk-away, better growth, decided by rubric not impulse
options.why: The pre-committed framework prevents desperation decisions — this is what it was for.

options.text: Hold out for a third offer
options.why: Bird-in-hand with a good rubric beats indefinite holding — decide and commit.

blocks.body: Discover → Model → Prove → Integrate → Operate → Generalize. Diagnose before prescribing.
applied→response→screen→onsite→offer. Fix the bottleneck stage, not everything.
Technical: depth + speed. Design: requirements first. Behavioral: STAR + numbers. Offers: walk-away pre-committed.
E/I S/N T/F J/P — preferences, not destiny. Energy economics for fit.
Pain + budget. MVP = riskiest-assumption test. LTV:CAC≥3, payback<12. Default alive.
SAFE: cap/discount. Dilution math. Raise from strength or don't raise.
Proof-level math → probability depth → Python/C++ → internships → MicroMasters → fork.
d(W²)=2WdW+dt. The chain rule for stochastic processes.

answerBank.a: FDE is a deployment model: you ship inside customer constraints and transfer operations. It suits people who like diagnosis, customers, and ambiguity. Pure SWE suits deep-system builders. The arc's skills transfer both ways.
Three excellent beats ten mediocre. Each with a README (problem, approach, results, proof link). Quality is the filter hiring managers actually apply.
It's a preference instrument, not a medical device — useful for working-style insight, not destiny. Use it for energy economics and team design; never for hiring decisions about others.
Default: job first, venture as the side project until unit economics or traction demand full time. Default alive applies to your life too — runway matters personally.
Desk quant roles hire at bachelor's/master's with proof-level math and C++/Python. Researcher roles skew PhD. The fork is real — audit honestly, then choose.

If you want the credential and the degree pathway: yes, with the transfer math done first. If you want only the knowledge: the preparation map (this module) plus the underlying math gets you most of the way.
